entries.title: Roy Cooper Flips a Key Senate Seat in North Carolina
entries.summary: The Democrat’s win in a battleground state is a major pickup for his party.
entries.content:
Democrat Roy Cooper is projected to win North Carolina’s open Senate seat in his race against Republican Michael Whatley.

Perhaps the most surprising element of the race was the lack of surprise in the ordinarily competitive state. Cooper, a popular former governor, pulled away from Whatley in polling and fundraising. As a result, national GOP attention shifted toward defending incumbents in states like Kansas and South Carolina.

Cooper’s win marks the first time a Democrat has won a North Carolina Senate seat since Kay Hagan’s 2008 victory, which was also the last time the state voted for a Democrat for president. Cooper will replace outgoing Sen. Thom Tillis, who publicly broke with Trump after deciding not to run for reelection. As elections become increasingly nationalized, North Carolina will become one of only a handful of states with one Democratic and one Republican senator.

Whatley was seeking elected office for the first time. He previously served as chair of the North Carolina Republican Party but is best known for his time as chair of the Republican National Committee. President Donald Trump and his allies aggressively pushed Whatley to run for the open Senate seat.

“I have a mission for my friends in North Carolina, and that is to get Michael Whatley to run for the U.S. Senate,” Trump posted on Truth Social days before Whatley formally joined the race. “HE WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN!”

Tillis endorsed Whatley but recently told Politico that “we needed probably a more moderate type of profile.”
APTOPIX Election 2026 North Carolina (3000x2000, AR: 1.50)Whatley spent his campaign touting Trump’s support. In the final months of the campaign, other Republican candidates grew more comfortable breaking with the president on immigration, the Iran war and the economy. Whatley, though, stuck close to Trump.

The situation looked so grim for Whatley that his campaign paused its airing of TV ads for two weeks in October.

Mid-October FEC filings show the Republican candidate raised just $13.7 million during the two-year election cycle, while Cooper raised nearly that much money in just the three-month period from July to September — and $47.2 million overall for the cycle.

That ultimately eased the path for Cooper, who ran an affordability-focused agenda and traveled the state on a “Make stuff cost less” tour. Cooper most recently served two terms as governor after a decades-long career in state electoral politics.

Cooper previously outperformed Democrats at the top of the ticket, winning gubernatorial elections in 2016 and 2020 even as the state voted for Trump in both elections.

As governor, Cooper set a record for the most vetoes in the state as he battled with the Republican-controlled state legislature. He focused on Medicaid expansion and public school funding, and he’s likely to deliver a reliable party-line vote for Democrats.
entries.author: Chase Pellegrini de Paur

entries.title: Democrat Chris Pappas Wins Election to U.S. Senate From New Hampshire
entries.summary: The race was one of a handful that will help determine which party controls the Senate.
entries.content:
By Holly Ramer

CONCORD, N.H. (AP) — U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas defeated former U.S. Sen. John E. Sununu in New Hampshire on Tuesday, keeping a critical open U.S. Senate seat under Democratic control.

The race to fill the seat being vacated by three-term Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen was one of a handful that could determine the balance of power in the Senate. Republicans were hoping to regain a foothold in a region long dominated by Democrats in Congress while Democrats sought to hold the seat as part of their effort to win control of the chamber.

While outsiders were on the ballot elsewhere, the race for the seat being vacated by Democrat Jeanne Shaheen featured two candidates who tried to tap into anti-establishment angst from the inside. Sununu railed against “career politicians” despite having spent three terms in the U.S. House and one in the Senate before being ousted by Shaheen in 2008. Pappas told voters “Our country is ready for change” while seeking to remain in Washington, where he has represented the state’s 1st Congressional District since 2019.

New Hampshire voters haven’t elected a Republican to Congress since 2010. They also have voted for Democrats for president since 2004, though Republicans have dominated at the state level in recent years. With the win, Pappas will become the first openly gay male U.S. senator.

Pappas, 46, grew up working in his family’s Manchester restaurant, which opened in 1917 and claims to have invented chicken tenders. After college, he served as a state lawmaker, county treasurer and state executive councilor before being elected to Congress. In September, he defeated a democratic socialist and other opponents by a wide margin to win the Democratic primary.

“This is a time for a new generation of leadership in the United States Senate who understands the problems New Hampshire is facing, who will stand up to the recklessness of this administration, lower costs and make life better for Granite Staters,” he said in a debate last week.

Pappas frequently sought to link Sununu to President Donald Trump, who endorsed Sununu despite Sununu once calling him a loser. He accused Sununu of having “a selective memory about what’s been going on over the last couple of years” and told him, “The guy who gave you his complete and total endorsement is wrecking New Hampshire’s Main Street economy.”

“This election is about Team New Hampshire versus Team Trump,” Pappas said. “This is not a moment to restore someone who was out of step with New Hampshire before and bring them back into power.”

Mike Bradley, 77, a licensed mental health counselor from Bow, described his vote for Pappas as “almost more anti- than pro-.”

“I’m so disgusted with what Republicans in general are doing with Trump at the helm, and pretty much no one’s standing up to him. The corruption, the homophobia, the transphobia, the endless war,” he said. “ I’m hoping that Democrats can grab a majority and counteract all this negative stuff.”

Sununu easily defeated former U.S. Sen. Scott Brown and a handful of lesser-known candidates to win the Republican nomination. His first name was conspicuously absent from his green, blue and white campaign signs, and critics said he was counting on voters confusing him with his popular younger brother, Chris Sununu, who served eight years as governor. Their father also is a former governor.

Once the Senate’s youngest member, Sununu is now 62, older than Shaheen was when he bragged in a campaign advertisement about being younger and faster than she was. He derided Pappas as an ineffective and out-of-touch “career politician” despite the fact that Sununu traveled a similar path from the House to the Senate and comes from a family whose name is synonymous with Republican politics in New Hampshire.

“Chris Pappas talks about all the things he wants to do and wants to accomplish, but he’s been there for eight years and he hasn’t gotten the job done,” Sununu said during the debate. “I’ll focus on the right issues. I’ll stand up to my party and the president when it’s right for New Hampshire, and I’ll get things done.”

Campaign cash poured in from all sides, though data compiled by AdImpact and OpenSecrets.org showed Republicans were spending considerably more as the race tightened.

Republicans accused Pappas of catering to Washington lobbyists and party bosses, describing the race as “problem solver Sununu” vs. “puppet Pappas.” “New Hampshire needs a leader, not a lightweight,” one ad from the National Republican Senatorial Committee concluded.

Pro-Pappas ads, meanwhile, accused Sununu of making millions off his political connections and highlighted the Sununu name appearing in the Epstein files. In a 2010 email, Jeffrey Epstein said Sununu “has good stories.” It’s unclear whether he meant the current candidate or his father, John H. Sununu, but Sununu says neither of them ever met or communicated with Epstein or the recipient of the email.

entries.title: Bookstore Owned by Sen. Wyden’s Wife to Pay $1.5M Over Pandemic Loan
entries.summary: The Strand Bookstore says the mistake was “unintentional” and that its accountant and lender were unaware of the restriction.
entries.content:
The Justice Department announced that a New York City bookstore owned by the wife of Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon will pay nearly $1.5 million to settle allegations it improperly obtained pandemic aid.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, accused Nancy Bass Wyden of lying on a February 2021 application to get a $932,350 second-round pandemic loan for her bookstore, despite rules passed by Congress barring such loans to businesses controlled by lawmakers or their spouses.

Ron Wyden, the Senate Finance Committee’s top Democrat, voted in favor of the legislation two months earlier.

Pirro said in a statement that the program was meant to save jobs, “not to enrich those who aren’t eligible for taxpayer-funded relief, especially the wife of a U.S. Senator.”

“No one gets a pass when it comes to defrauding the American taxpayer,” she added.

The Strand Bookstore told CNBC the mistake was “unintentional” and that its accountant and lender were unaware of the restriction.

The $1.5 million civil settlement resolves a whistleblower lawsuit under the False Claims Act. Blockquote Inc., which brought the case, will receive approximately $148,256 from the settlement.

entries.title: Jon Ossoff, a Possible 2028 Presidential Candidate, Is Reelected to the Senate
entries.summary: The Georgia senator easily defeated Republican Rep. Mike Collins.
entries.content:
Sen. Jon Ossoff is projected to easily win reelection in the battleground state of Georgia, defeating Republican Rep. Mike Collins.

Ossoff will enter his second term widely viewed as a potential 2028 presidential contender, given his track record as a prodigious fundraiser who has now twice pulled off statewide wins in a state where President Donald Trump has also won twice.

He has, however, repeatedly denied any interest in seeking the White House and promised to serve a full Senate term if reelected.

Ossoff far outspent his opponent and led in the polls throughout the campaign.

The senator has been a messaging leader for Democrats this cycle — he was early to adopt a populist focus on corruption, coined the term “Epstein class” and helped make Trump aide Natalie Harp a recognizable figure.

“Ossoff, especially when we are in a moment where a lot of the Democratic base and a lot of the Democratic electorate are hungry for a new generation of leadership … that just on paper creates an extremely compelling figure,” said Andrew Heaton, a Georgia Democratic operative. “Then throw in just how great of a speaker he is, how sharp he is.”

Collins, who won a competitive Republican primary with Trump’s endorsement by touting his MAGA bona fides, gambled on a base-turnout strategy by defending the Trump administration.

The lawmaker has a long history of posting inflammatory content on his X account and during the campaign faced a string of scandals involving his staff and family members’ ties to far-right views.

Ossoff framed his opponent as a “bigot” and in a debate said Collins had “hired half the Third Reich” to staff his office.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club,” Ossoff said in the debate, invoking the late Georgia lawmaker and civil rights leader.

Collins’ failure to break through led national Republicans to abandon him — they deployed ad money to states seen as more winnable instead.

Georgia Republican operative Heath Garrett said that Collins’ brand as a MAGA warrior from rural Georgia was a mismatch for independents and swing voters.

“He's struggled to identify with and brand himself, in the suburban and urban areas along the coast and in the metro Atlanta area, because his personality and style don't necessarily fit those voters,” Garrett said.

Meanwhile, Ossoff’s efforts to cultivate relationships across party lines helped the incumbent woo Republicans.

“He has been methodical about working with elected officials in the smallest cities and counties throughout the state and trying to find ways to be helpful to them,” Garrett said. “And at the end of the day, constituent services still matter in politics, particularly in close elections.”
entries.author: Hunter Riggall
